name: How Biases Compound
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: How Six Small Biases Add Up to One Big Bet
lesson.summary: Cognitive biases rarely operate alone inside an organization, in practice they form a reinforcing loop where each one makes the next one easier to fall into, turning a series of individually modest errors into one large, hard-to-reverse collective bet.
lesson.body:
Every bias covered so far in this book has been explained mostly in isolation, one mechanism at a time, for clarity. Real institutional decisions rarely work that way. Inside an actual organization deciding how much to invest in quantum computing, these biases interact and reinforce each other, and the compounded version is considerably more powerful, and more resistant to correction, than any single bias operating alone would be.

The loop typically starts with anchoring bias, an early cost estimate or timeline projection, often optimistic even at the outset, becomes the reference point against which every later update gets measured, regardless of how much new information has since arrived. Once real money has been committed against that anchor, sunk cost fallacy makes abandoning it feel costly in a way that has nothing to do with the forward-looking merits of continuing. Meanwhile confirmation bias shapes what gets noticed and reported internally, teams and leaders naturally pay closer attention to results consistent with the original bet and give less airtime to results that complicate it, not out of dishonesty but because that is how attention and memory work under motivated reasoning.

As more institutions publicly announce quantum computing programs, the bandwagon effect kicks in, the sheer fact that so many credible organizations are investing gets treated as evidence of underlying value, even when each individual organization's decision was influenced by watching the others rather than by independent technical assessment. This is reinforced by what might be called FOMO in quantum computing investment specifically, the fear that sitting out a potentially transformative technology is the larger risk, which can push organizations to invest defensively, to avoid being left behind, rather than because their own analysis showed a clearly positive expected return.

Optimism bias then colors how ambiguous technical results get interpreted at every stage of this loop. An incremental engineering milestone, a modest reduction in error rate or a new record qubit count, gets read internally and externally as confirmation that the original timeline was basically right, rather than as one small data point among many. That confident interpretation feeds back into the anchor for the next round of funding decisions, often at a higher baseline than before, and the entire loop restarts one level up.

The systemic danger here is that no single actor in this loop necessarily needs to be irrational in isolation. An investor who joins because credible peers already joined, a researcher who emphasizes positive results because that is what gets published and funded, an executive who defends a past investment rather than reopening a settled question, none of these individual choices requires believing anything false. Yet the aggregate effect can end up substantially detached from the underlying technical reality covered in earlier chapters, narrow applicability, an ambiguous improvement curve, and a missing wave of complementary innovation. Recognizing the compounding structure itself, not just any one bias in isolation, is what actually allows an organization to interrupt the loop before the collective bet grows larger than the evidence can support.
